newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-SAMPRAS GETS COMFORTABLE AGAIN ON GRASS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS GETS COMFORTABLE AGAIN ON GRASS.

text.p: Pete Sampras is thumping down serves and punching back volleys on the manicured lawns of the Hurlingham club this week in the hope of getting his grass legs back in time for his assault on the Wimbledon title.

The American world number one and three-times Wimbledon champion possesses a near-perfect grass-court game but he showed last week when he lost in the quarter-finals at Queen's that he was out of touch with the surface.
"I was disappointed -- it was a match I felt I should have won," said Sampras who remains the firm Wimbledon favourite despite that defeat and his third-round exit at the French Open last month.

After a long hard-court and clay-court season it is difficult to adapt to the fast, slippery English lawns and with so few grass tournaments in the professional calendar there is little opportunity for practice before the most prestigious grand slam of them all.

"The difference between clay and grass is night and day -- the whole mentality, the surface speed, you couldn't find a more drastic change than that," said Sampras who will be top seed next week for the fourth time in five years.
Despite his recent disappointments Sampras, who says he has learned to love grass, is in confident mood.

"I'm not in a panic. I know I can get better before Wimbledon," said Sampras, who since winning his first 17 matches of the year including the Australian Open has slumped to a 6-7 win-loss tally. "If I worried about all my defeats I'd be in an institution by now."
Several top players whose skills were honed on slow red clay have decided that trying to adapt to the serve-and-volley game is too much of a struggle.
Sergi Bruguera, French Open former champion and this year's runner-up, heads a list of top 20 Spaniards who have not entered or have pulled out of the championships.

Their departure leaves the field open for the big hitters such as second-seeded Croat Goran Ivanisevic, twice a Wimbledon finalist, and Australian Queen's winner Mark Philippoussis, who finds himself promoted to the seventh seed from a world ranking of 13.
Other clay-courters are making a game stab at the grass.

"We have no grass courts in Chile," said world number 10 Marcelo Rios after losing in the first round of the pre-Wimbledon Nottingham tournament on Monday. "I agree with players who say grass is for cows and playing football....but I will try my best at Wimbledon."
Newly-crowned French Open champion Gustavo Kuerten of Brazil also had a torrid time in his first grass tournament, losing 6-1 7-5 to Britain's Greg Rusedski at Nottingham.

It was a tough draw for the 19-year-old, playing a man whose serve has been timed at 223 kph, second only to Philippoussis on the circuit. As luck would have it, Rusedski and Philippoussis have been drawn to meet each other in the first round at Wimbledon.

"I just did not know how to play," Kuerten said. Few reckon Kuerten, seeded 11, will get far at Wimbledon where he meets emerging American Justin Gimelstob in the first round and is in the same quarter of the draw as 1991 champion Michael Stich and title holder Richard Krajicek, the 1.96-metre Dutch power generator who put out Sampras last year.

Michael Chang will also be giving Wimbledon his best shot. Though he is physically unsuited to the grass game, standing more than 20 cms shorter than Krajicek, and has been seeded five as opposed to his world ranking of two, the American former French Open champion wants Wimbledon more than any other title.
"In part because it's such a prestigious event and partly because people don't think I can win it." Chang said.
Chang went out in his first match at Queen's but is playing a grass tournament in the Netherlands, where he got past the first hurdle and is training hard this week.
He has no easy Wimbledon draw, meeting Todd Woodbridge, who with Mark Woodforde has won the doubles title for the last four years, in the first round.

If the draw holds true and Chang matches his previous best of reaching the quarter-finals, he will meet Russian Yevgeny Kafelnikov, last year's French Open champion and winner of last week's Halle grass tournament, in which he beat Boris Becker in the semifinals and Petr Korda in a tight final.
Kafelnikov, seeded third at Wimbledon and nicknamed Kalashnikov for the ferocity of his shots, is joining Sampras at Hurlingham this week for a work-out away from the stresses of the tour.

Becker, champion in 1985 and twice since and a favourite with the crowds, has been promoted to eighth seed despite a disappointing injury-prone season which has seen him drop to 18 in the ranking. He is scheduled to meet Sampras in the quarter-finals.

But the projected quarter-final clash with the most venom promises to be that between Ivanisevic, desperate for the title after coming so close, and Philippoussis, the up-and-coming hitter who beat him in straight sets at the Queen's final.
That 57-minute match, boasting 27 aces and only five rallies of more than four shots, showed what physique, racket technology and power can do to the men's game of tennis when the surface is fast.
It is just as well not every Wimbledon entrant is built for grass.
